CausalChain: Metabolic stress in cancer cells -> Decreased NSUN2 activity and reduced m5C modification -> Increased tRNA susceptibility to cleavage by angiogenin -> Accumulation of specific tRFs -> tRFs interact with translation initiation factors and promote ribosome biogenesis -> Selective translation of survival and metabolic adaptation genes -> Enhanced tumor cell survival under metabolic stress
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that under metabolic stress, cancer cells experience a decline in NSUN2-mediated m5C methylation, which predisposes tRNAs to angiogenin-mediated cleavage and leads to the production of a defined subset of tRNA-derived fragments. These fragments act as a molecular switch by specifically modulating the translation machinery — they displace key initiation factors and stimulate ribosome biogenesis, thereby driving the selective translation of mRNAs encoding survival and metabolic adaptation proteins. To rigorously test this model, we will leverage advanced technologies, including high-throughput RNA sequencing for tRF identification, ribosome profiling to detect shifts in translational output, and CRISPR methodologies to perturb the epitranscriptomic landscape, enabling a precise causal mapping of the pathway.
Abstract: Under metabolic stress, cancer cells exhibit reduced NSUN2 activity leading to a decrease in m5C modifications on tRNAs. This epitranscriptomic alteration increases tRNA susceptibility to cleavage by angiogenin, thereby generating a specific subset of tRNA-derived fragments (tRFs). Our hypothesis posits that these tRFs act as molecular switches by binding to and displacing key translation initiation factors and promoting ribosome biogenesis. This reprograms the translational machinery in favor of selectively translating survival and metabolic adaptation genes. Importantly, we propose utilizing contemporary technologies such as high-throughput RNA sequencing, ribosome profiling, and CRISPR-based editing to accurately map the tRF interactome and validate their mechanistic role in cancer cell adaptation. This integrative approach not only reinforces the original causal chain but also provides a robust, testable framework for potential therapeutic targeting in oncology.
Orignal_vs_New: The new hypothesis retains the original causal chain—linking metabolic stress, loss of m5C modification, and tRNA cleavage to tRF-mediated translational reprogramming—while refining mechanistic details. It explicitly defines the roles of NSUN2 activity loss and angiogenin-mediated cleavage, and further elucidates how tRFs interact with translation initiation factors and ribosome biogenesis to promote survival. Additionally, the revised version integrates contemporary technological approaches (RNA sequencing, ribosome profiling, and CRISPR-based editing) to enhance experimental tractability and strengthen the testability of the hypothesis.
